info.title: Ianua Identity Provider API
info.description:
Ianua is a **multi-tenant identity provider** with an integrated **zero-trust proxy**.
This API covers everything you operate it with: authentication, authorization, OAuth2,
SAML/OIDC federation, organization and tenant management, routing and policy for the
proxy, webhooks, messaging, and real-time event streams.

## Identity planes

Endpoints are scoped to one of three planes, from widest to narrowest:

- **Platform** — operators who run the deployment itself. Manage organizations,
  operators, and impersonation. Paths under `/api/v1/operators` and `/api/v1/organizations`.
- **Organization** — owners and members who administer a customer organization and its
  tenants through the dashboard. Paths under `/api/v1/organizations/{org_slug}/…`.
- **Tenant** — the end users that an organization's tenants serve. Paths under
  `/api/v1/organizations/{org_slug}/tenants/{tenant_slug}/…`.

A request can only reach what its plane allows; anything more returns `403`.

## Authentication

All authenticated requests use a **bearer token**:

```
Authorization: Bearer <session-token>
```

Obtain one by logging in:

- **Organization users** → `POST /api/v1/login` with `{ "email", "password" }`.
- **Tenant users** → `POST /api/v1/organizations/{org_slug}/tenants/{tenant_slug}/login`.

Both return a `refresh_token` — use it as the bearer token above. Some operations require
multi-factor authentication or a stepped-up session and will respond `401` until satisfied.

## Conventions

- **Pagination** — list endpoints accept `offset` and `limit` (max 100) and return
  `{ items, total, offset, limit, has_next }`.
- **Sorting** — `?sort=-created_at,name` (prefix `-` for descending). Allowed fields are
  listed in each `sort` parameter's description.
- **Timestamps** — RFC 3339 / ISO 8601 (e.g. `2026-07-01T14:22:09Z`).
- **Errors** — a consistent envelope: `{ "error", "message", "details" }`. Common statuses:
  `401` unauthenticated, `403` forbidden, `404` not found, `409` conflict, `422` validation,
  `429` rate limited.

## Real-time

Endpoints under the **Real-time** tag are **WebSocket** upgrades (documented with a `101`
response). Connect with a WebSocket client and the same bearer token to receive live
notification and dashboard streams.

post.summary: Log in as an organization user
post.description:
The front door to the management dashboard. Authenticates an
**organization user** (owner or member) with email and password.
This is the only login that is *not* tenant-scoped — there is no org
or tenant slug in the path.

On success you get a session: a `session_id`, a `refresh_token` to
send as your `Authorization: Bearer` token, and the resolved org and
tenant context. If the same email belongs to more than one tenant,
the response is a **tenant picker** instead — choose one and log in
again with `tenant_slug` set.

If the account has MFA enrolled, the response sets `mfa_required:
true` and the session stays limited until you complete the step-up at
`…/auth/mfa/verify`.

**Session status.** On success a session is created **`Active`**. From there it
can only move `Active → Suspended` (risk or binding violation — needs re-auth to
resume) or `Active → Revoked` (logout, token theft — terminal). Expiry is
time-based and separate from status: a session can be `Active` yet expired.

post.description:
Emergency access for when normal authorization is in the way of an
active incident. Mints a **time-boxed** elevated grant so an operator
can act during an outage or security event.

Break-glass is deliberately loud, not a backdoor: every grant is
fully audited with who, why, and for how long, and it expires on its
own. Revoke it early at the break-glass revoke endpoint once the
incident is contained.

Ends an active emergency grant immediately, before its natural
expiry. Call this the moment elevated access is no longer needed —
the shorter the window, the smaller the blast radius.

The revocation is audited alongside the original grant, closing the
loop on the incident. Revoking an already-expired or already-revoked
grant is a no-op.

Returns the devices the signed-in user has marked as trusted. A
trusted device can skip MFA step-up for the duration of the tenant's
trust window, so this list is effectively the set of places that get
the fast path.

Treat it as a security surface: anything unfamiliar here should be
revoked at the device-revoke endpoint. Entries expire on their own
once the trust window lapses.

**Device status.** Lists only devices in **`Trusted`** status — the ones eligible
to skip MFA. A device drops off this list the moment it's `Revoked`.

Marks the current device as trusted so future logins from it can skip
MFA step-up until the tenant's trust window expires. This is the
"remember this device" checkbox on the login screen.

Trust is a convenience traded against risk — only offer it on devices
the user controls, never shared or public machines. The grant is
scoped to this user and can be pulled at any time from the device
list.

**Device status.** Registers the device in **`Trusted`** status, letting it skip
MFA within the trust window. The only transition out is `Trusted → Revoked`.

Removes trust from a device. The next login from it has to pass full
MFA step-up again — the fast path is gone.

Use this the instant a device is lost, sold, or looks unfamiliar in
the trusted list. Revocation takes effect immediately and is scoped
to the signed-in user's own devices.

**Device status.** Moves the device `Trusted → Revoked`. `Revoked` is terminal — a
revoked device is treated as unknown on the next login and must be trusted again
from scratch.

Revokes the current session so its refresh token can no longer be
used. Idempotent — logging out an already-revoked session still
returns `204`.

Only this session is ended; the user's other active sessions (other
devices, browsers) keep working. Revoke those separately.

**Session status.** Moves the session `Active → Revoked`. `Revoked` is terminal —
the session can never be reactivated, so the user signs in again for a new one.

delete.summary: Disable (unenroll) the current tenant user's MFA.
delete.description:
Removes the caller's active MFA enrollment. If the tenant's policy
requires MFA, the user is prompted to re-enroll on next login.

post.description:
Begins enrolling an authenticator app (TOTP). Returns a freshly
generated secret as an `otpauth://` URI — render it as a QR code for
the user to scan with Google Authenticator, 1Password, Authy, or any
compatible app.

Enrollment isn't active yet: the secret stays pending until the user
proves they scanned it by confirming a code at the enroll-confirm
endpoint. Call this again to rotate the pending secret.

**Enrollment status.** Creates (or resets) the enrollment in **`Pending`** —
started but not yet usable. It only becomes active after `Pending → Verified` at
the confirm step.

Activates the pending authenticator by verifying a code it produced.
A correct code proves the secret was scanned successfully and flips
MFA on for the account.

The response includes a set of **one-time recovery codes** — the only
time they're ever shown. Store them somewhere safe; they're the way
back in if the authenticator device is lost. A wrong or stale code
returns `401` and leaves enrollment pending.

**Enrollment status.** A valid code moves the enrollment `Pending → Verified`, and
MFA is now active for the account. Turning MFA off later is `Verified → Disabled`;
re-enrolling is `Disabled → Pending`.

Completes a step-up challenge. When a login returns `mfa_required:
true`, the session is limited until the user submits a valid code
from their authenticator app here.

A correct code promotes the session to fully authenticated. Codes are
time-based and short-lived; a wrong or expired code returns `401`.
Repeated failures count toward the tenant's lockout policy. No
authenticator handy? Use a recovery code instead.

**Enrollment status.** Only a **`Verified`** enrollment can answer a step-up
challenge — a `Pending` or `Disabled` one cannot. This endpoint doesn't change the
enrollment status; it clears the session's step-up requirement.

Begins a passwordless sign-in with a registered passkey. Returns a
one-time challenge for the browser's `navigator.credentials.get()`
call, which the user satisfies with a biometric or security-key tap.

The challenge is short-lived and single-use. Pass the browser's
assertion response to the login-confirm endpoint to complete
authentication and receive a session.

Completes a passwordless sign-in. Submit the assertion from the
browser's `navigator.credentials.get()` call; the server verifies the
signature against the stored credential and the challenge issued at
start.

On success you get a session and a `refresh_token`, exactly like a
password login — but nothing phishable ever crossed the wire. A
replayed, expired, or unrecognized assertion returns `401`.

Begins registering a WebAuthn passkey — a phishing-resistant
credential backed by the device's secure hardware (Touch ID, Face ID,
Windows Hello, a security key). Returns a one-time challenge for the
browser's `navigator.credentials.create()` call.

Nothing is stored yet: the challenge is bound to this user and
expires quickly. Hand the browser's attestation response to the
register-confirm endpoint to finish.

Finishes enrolling a passkey. Submit the attestation response from
the browser's `navigator.credentials.create()` call; the server
verifies it against the challenge issued at start and stores the
resulting public-key credential.

From here on, the user can sign in with the passkey — no password to
phish, no shared secret to leak. A mismatched or expired challenge is
rejected.

Updates the signed-in user's password. Requires the **current**
password as proof — knowing a live session isn't enough, so a stolen
token alone can't lock the real owner out.

The new password must satisfy the tenant's password policy (length,
complexity, reuse history). On success, other active sessions may be
revoked depending on tenant policy, forcing a fresh login elsewhere.

Finishes the forgot-password flow. Present the token from the reset
email together with a new password. The token is single-use and
expires quickly — a used, expired, or forged token returns `401`.

The new password must meet the tenant's password policy. On success
the password is replaced and existing sessions are revoked, so every
device has to sign in again with the new credentials.

Kicks off the forgot-password flow. If the email maps to a real
account, a time-limited, single-use reset link is sent to it.

The response is **always** `204`, whether or not the address exists —
the endpoint never reveals which emails are registered. Complete the
flow at the reset-confirm endpoint with the token from the email.

The fallback for MFA when the authenticator device is lost or
unavailable. Satisfies a step-up challenge using one of the recovery
codes issued at enrollment instead of a TOTP code.

Recovery codes are **single-use** — redeeming one burns it, and the
remaining count drops by one. When they run low, the user should
re-enroll to generate a fresh set. An unknown or already-used code
returns `401`.

The Assertion Consumer Service endpoint for SAML single sign-on. The
identity provider redirects the browser here with a signed assertion
after the user authenticates on the IdP's side.

The assertion's signature, issuer, audience, and validity window are
all verified before any session is minted — an unsigned, expired, or
misaddressed assertion is rejected. On success the user is signed in
under the mapped tenant. This endpoint is called by the browser, not
invoked directly by API clients.

Re-scopes the current session to a different tenant the user already
belongs to — no password re-entry, no new login. This powers the
tenant switcher for people who work across several tenants in the
same organization.

Membership is re-checked on switch: you can only move to a tenant the
user is actually a member of, otherwise the request is denied. The
target tenant's own MFA and policy rules then apply to the re-scoped
session.

**Session status.** The existing **`Active`** session is re-scoped to the new
tenant; its status is unchanged. The target tenant's MFA rules may still apply
before the re-scoped session is fully usable.

Trades a valid `refresh_token` for a fresh one and extends the
session. Refresh tokens are **single-use**: each call rotates the
token, so the one you send is immediately invalidated and replaced by
the one you get back. Store the new token and discard the old.

If a token is ever replayed after rotation, the whole session is
treated as compromised and revoked. A revoked, expired, or unknown
token returns `401` — log in again.

**Session status.** The session stays **`Active`** while its token rotates. A
`Suspended` session can't refresh until the user clears step-up; a `Revoked`
session is gone for good and returns `401`.

post.description:
Authenticates an **end user** inside a specific tenant with email and
password. This is the login your tenants' own users go through.

Unknown organization, unknown tenant, unknown email, and wrong
password all return the **same** error — by design, so the endpoint
can't be used to probe which accounts exist. On success you receive a
session and a `refresh_token` for the bearer header.

Subject to the tenant's password policy, IP allow-list, and lockout
rules: too many failed attempts lock the account for the tenant's
configured lockout window.

**Session status.** Creates a session in **`Active`** status. It later moves to
`Suspended` (risk step-up) or `Revoked` (logout or token theft — terminal, never
reactivated). Expiry is time-based, tracked separately from status.

ApiKeyId.description:
Globally unique identifier for an API key.

API keys are a first-class authentication method for M2M access,
separate from OAuth clients. Each key has a unique `ApiKeyId`
used internally, plus a `key_prefix` for O(1) lookup and a
hashed secret for verification.

ApiKeyStatus.description:
Operational status of an API key.

Valid transitions:
- `Active` → `Revoked` (admin revokes, security incident)
- `Active` → `Expired` (past expiration date)
- `Expired` → `Revoked` (admin cleanup)

`Revoked` is terminal — revoked keys cannot be reactivated.

AssuranceLevel.description:

Classifies how strongly the system has verified the user's

stronger authentication factors.

Routes and resources can require a minimum AAL. If the user's
session doesn't meet the required level, the proxy forces
step-up authentication (e.g. prompt for MFA to elevate from
AAL1 to AAL2).

CustomPermission.description:
Customer-defined permission for their own application.

The `IdP` stores these in roles and includes them in JWT claims,
but never interprets them. The customer's application reads
the token and enforces access based on these.

# Validation

Both resource and action are validated on construction:
- ASCII only, lowercase alphanumeric + hyphens + underscores + `*` (wildcard)
- 1–64 characters each
- Cannot start with `idp:` (reserved for system permissions)
- No control characters, spaces, or injection-prone characters

# Examples

```
# use ianua_domain::domains::authorization::permission::CustomPermission;
let perm = CustomPermission::new("project", "write").unwrap();
assert_eq!(perm.to_string(), "project:write");
```

MigrationStatus.description:
Lifecycle status of an algorithm migration.

Valid transitions:
- `Planned` → `InProgress` (new key created with target algorithm)
- `Planned` → `Cancelled` (plan abandoned before any keys created)
- `InProgress` → `Validating` (target key promoted to primary signer)
- `InProgress` → `RolledBack` (migration aborted, reverted to source)
- `Validating` → `Completed` (source key revoked, migration done)
- `Validating` → `RolledBack` (issues found, reverted to source)

Terminal states: `Completed`, `RolledBack`, `Cancelled`.

SystemPermission.description:
`IdP`-managed permissions for tenant administration operations.

Grouped by domain. Each domain has a `Manage` variant that implies
all fine-grained actions, plus individual action variants for
custom roles.

Tenant admins assign these to roles. Users inherit permissions
from their roles. The UI renders groups with a "Manage (all)"
toggle and individual checkboxes underneath.

# Delegation rule

A user can only grant permissions they themselves hold.
`Manage` holders can grant any action in that domain.
Fine-grained holders can only grant exactly what they have.

tags.name: Authentication
tags.description:
Everything about proving **who** is calling: password and passkey login, MFA step-up,
session refresh, recovery, device trust, tenant switching, and emergency break-glass access.

Several of these endpoints move a resource through a small **status lifecycle** — a session,
an MFA enrollment, a trusted device. Where that applies, the endpoint documents the status it
lands the resource in and which transitions are legal, so you always know where you stand.

## Ground rules

- Login responses never reveal whether an email exists — unknown account and wrong password
  look identical.
- Refresh tokens are single-use; replaying a rotated token revokes the entire session.
- Recovery codes and trusted-device grants are single-use and revocable.
